Figure 1:Transforming foundation model embeddings into engines of clinical discovery.aGlyph can be applied to any data expected to contain useful markers for discovery.bFoundation models compress multimodal clinical data into high-dimensional embeddings, typically used for predefined prediction tasks.
The structural contents of embeddings driving these predictions is typically not unexplored.cGlyph instead transforms FM embeddings into engines for discovery, mapping a space of concepts hidden within these embeddings.
Glyph goes beyond embeddings by decomposing them into sparse concepts that can be studied individually and in selected combinations (Figure1c).dGlyph concepts recover associations established in clinical research and ICD-based PheWAS analyses, while revealing complementary associations not yet discovered by either approach.e–fGlyph evaluates concepts foreassociations with future disease after correction for multiple testing,fassociations that persist after adjustment for measured confounders, andgclinical interpretability.hAll findings are tested for reproducibility across multiple cohorts.iValidated concepts provide an interface for asking complex questions of FM embeddings and grounding the answers in the underlying data.

Figure 2:The Glyph framework. An interactive version is available athttps://stanfordmimi.github.io/Glyph-research/.aAt the Discovery Site, Glyph trains sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to decompose foundation model (FM) embeddings into sparse concepts.bEach SAE encoder is then frozen as a concept extractor and its decoder discarded.
Concepts are re-extracted zero-shot in held-out internal and external cohorts to assess reproducibility of their interpretations, prognostic associations, and confounder analyses.cThe discovered concept space maps the clinical characteristics and disease burden of patients undergoing abdominal CT at the Discovery Site, alongside routine variables such as age and smoking status.
We show 397 concepts (9.26% of the 4,285 candidate features) that were associated with at least one of the 141 prognostic outcomes after Bonferroni correction.
Edges show correlations between concepts in the top 2.5%.
Clinically related concepts were found to cluster into subregions (dashed boxes) corresponding to liver, renal, and cardiovascular disease, and systemic inflammatory and cholestatic illness.
Node size scales with the logarithm of the number of patients who share the specific concept.
A confounder-adjusted version of this network is shown in Figure11.

Figure 3:Glyph concept-wide association study.aEach Glyph concept is tested for association to each of 141 future disease outcomes within 1 to 4 years, yielding 604,185 concept-outcome pairs evaluated using per-standard-deviation odds ratios.bADiscovery filter(p≤0.05p\leq 0.05adjusted for multiple testing via Bonferroni correction, equivalent top≤8.28×10−8p\leq 8.28\times 10^{-8}, and OR>1.0>1.0) applied on the Discovery Site yields 4,463 (0.739%) promising associations.cNumber of promising associations per modality on the Discovery Site, totalling 4,463; these are fixed and tested for reproducibility without calibration on the Internal Test, External Site #1, and External Site #2 cohorts using a 5% FDR threshold (Benjamini–Hochberg), with the percentage replicating shown per modality and cohort.dVolcano plot of all concept-outcome associations and the Discovery filter selection.eRisk profiles and reproducibility statistics for one organ-specific and one systemic-risk concept.f–hSample counts and observed probabilities of future disease onset, with confidence intervals, across concept-activation bins.

Figure 4:Confounder-adjusted association study.aGlyph concepts act as variables that can be compared with one another and with established clinical variables in a unified feature space, enabling confounder analysis of FM predictions.bFor each of the 4,463 promising associations, the ten most strongly associated concepts across other modalities are automatically selected as candidate confounders, alongside six universal clinical covariates.cNumber of associations per modality retaining a significant, adjusted OR>1.0>1.0after confounder adjustment per site.d–gAssociation profiles show that after adjustment I21 (ascites) loses most associations, L127 (cytopenia) remains broadly associated, R85 (cirrhotic liver morphology and varices) retains hepatic associations, and I26 (aortic atherosclerosis) retains cardiovascular and neurocognitive associations.hAn example of a knowledge-guided confounder analysis for primary liver cancer.

Figure 5:Glyph identifies associations beyond the clinical literature and adds prognostic value.aScreening 342,647 PubMed papers across 21 outcomes yielded 294 representative studies and 412 literature-derived predictors.bAdding ten Glyph concepts per outcome improved held-out AUC beyond literature markers, with the largest gains in metabolic, haematologic, and infectious outcomes.cOn average, Glyph concepts outperform literature markers, even when top performing markers are selected on the Discovery Set.dGlyph concepts provide discoveries that complement the history of clinical research.
The additional prognostic benefit varied across axes, as illustrated by the improvement for HFpEF (top) and the larger gain for sepsis (bottom).

Figure 6:The MCP enables more complex analyses that build on a foundational layer of Glyph concepts. In this example, concepts were combined into nodes that competed against one as independent predictors for inclusion in a disease model of septicemia. I76 (an undocumented imaging concept linked to septicemia) provided a predictive contribution independent of hepatic disease markers, fluid accumulation, BMI, inflammatory markers, malignancy, and evidence of clinical intervention, and contributed to prognostic AUC predictive across three cohorts.

Figure 7:a,Outcomes were selected by ranking Phecode prediction AUCs on the Discovery Site validation set.
After excluding non-disease codes, 141 of the top 150 outcomes were retained.
Without refitting, imaging probes transferred with minimal loss across cohorts, whereas report performance declined at External Site #2.b,SAEs fitted at the Discovery Site were applied unchanged across cohorts.
Reconstruction remained high for imaging and labs but declined steadily for reports.c,Replacing dense embeddings with sparse concepts preserved most predictive information, with less loss for imaging than reports.d,Median odds ratios of significant associations followed a similar per-site trend to the predictive performance, maintaining high OR for imaging- and labs-derived concepts and steadily dropping for radiology report-derived concepts.

Figure 8:The Glyph MCP brings a new capability; the ability to immediately perform, user-specified requests about high-dimensional unstructured data, such as imaging. Here, Claude Code returns the most highly associated concepts for future risk of myocardial infarction, the majority of which are labs concepts. Responses are grounded by the Glyph layer.

Figure 9:Glyph generates individualised risk explanations for a given outcome. For a query patient (AC42403ee, 74.9% predicted CKD risk, 93.6th percentile), the system surfaces the concepts most responsible for that prediction alongside their attribution scores, activation levels, and population rarity. Cross-referencing against the top population-level risk features reveals which epidemiologically validated signals are active in this patient, grounding the individual explanation in cohort-level evidence.

Figure 10:The Glyph concept layer is flexible to other forms of discovery beyond prognosis. Here, Glyph performs a patients-like-me scenario where the most similar patient to a query is found. Their similarity is then explained in terms of shared concepts, and the rarity of such a co-occurrence at their respective levels of activation.

Figure 11:Confounder-adjusted inter-concept associations.aThe full adjusted network. Edges denote directed dependencies from the fitted sparse SEM, retained where the standardized coefficient exceeds|w|≥0.1|w|\geq 0.1; edge width scales with|w||w|and colour denotes sign (red positive, blue negative). Dashed edges involve at least one undocumented concept.bConcepts within two degrees of separation from liver cirrhosis (R85), a disease hub known to link to splenomegaly (I65) and portal hypertension (R309).cPatient age shows adjusted associations with many concepts, particularly cardiovascular disease and spinal degeneration (R1).dIn this abdominal CT cohort, labs indicating cholestasis (L108) form the major bridge between modalities, connecting abnormal lab states, such as elevated alkaline phosphatase (L33) and cytopenia (L127), to structural imaging phenotypes such as splenomegaly (I65) and intra-abdominal fluid (I105).

Figure 12:Glyph concepts are automatically extracted, interpreted, and
reproduced zero-shot at external sites.
Each concept is interpreted on the Discovery Site by comparing top- versus non-activating examples, then re-extracted at an Internal Test cohort and two external sites where the same interpretation is re-tested on unseen patients; consistent discrimination shows both concepts and interpretations transfer across institutions.a–cA radiology report concept, labeledmetastatic disease, re-extracted zero-shot and confirmed at every site. AutoInterp accuracy is highest for reports: as human-written summaries, their concepts are near-fully interpretable but bounded in discovery potential.d–eAn imaging concept whose interpretation is not consistently documented in radiology reports, yet was found to rank among the top 10% of imaging predictors of infection, sepsis, wasting, and organ failure.fRemarkably, 52.5% of imaging concepts were interpretable via corresponding radiology reports.g–iA laboratory concept, labelledmonocytosis or neutrophilia, confirmed across sites.

Figure 13:Glyph concepts build on pre-coded discovery.Phecodes group ICD codes into manually curated, clinically meaningful concepts for use in research[2].
We test complementary benefits of data-driven Glyph concepts over Phecodes.a–bBinary Phecodes drawn from the full recorded history yield 3.4×\timesmore significant associations than Glyph concepts, but reproduce less often at Internal Test (49% versus 69%) and have a smaller median effect (OR 1.33 versus 1.45).
Recent Phecodes, restricted to the scan-adjacent window, also yield more associations than Glyph concepts but reproduce less often.cDirectly corresponding Phecodes were often less specific than imaging- or laboratory-derived Glyph concepts and yielded weaker or nonsignificant associations.
In other cases, the broader clinical history captured by Phecodes provided a stronger proxy for future risk.
For example, hypertension served as a proxy for atherosclerosis (bottom) and outperformed the corresponding Glyph concept for some outcomes.

Figure 14:Architectural ablation of the sparse autoencoder across 141 disease prediction tasks. Results are organized by modality, with panelsa–ccorresponding to CT imaging (Merlin), radiology reports (Qwen3-Embedding-8B), and laboratory values (Labs FM), respectively. Within each modality, results are organized by metric, showing sparse autoencoder reconstruction loss (MSE),R2R^{2}between original and reconstructed foundation-model embeddings, and mean downstream AUC across the 141 disease prediction tasks. Reconstruction loss andR2R^{2}are evaluated on the discovery training set and unseen external data, while downstream AUC assesses whether the Glyph concept space preserves the predictive performance of the underlying foundation models with minimal degradation. Across modalities, diminishing returns in reconstruction are observed beyondK=40K=40, withR2R^{2}improving and subsequently plateauing at this sparsity level.
